hero.body: I am an Account Executive in Singapore who spends the day selling complex software and the night turning AI ideas into working tools. This portfolio is where those two sides meet: commercial discipline, practical curiosity, and a bias toward shipping.

paragraphs: At work, I use AI to make sales preparation sharper: researching accounts, understanding personas, finding buying signals, and turning messy information into a clearer point of view before customer conversations.

Outside work, I build small products around real problems in my own life, from interview-practice tools to household operations. I care less about demos that sound impressive and more about systems that survive real use.

intro: Before sales, there was a monk, a commando and a coach.

My career has not followed a conventional path. Each chapter taught me something I still rely on today: discipline, composure under pressure, clear communication and responsibility for the people around me.

I eventually found my way into enterprise technology sales, progressing from SDR to Majors Account Executive at DocuSign through four promotions in five years. Today, I am applying the same learning velocity to AI, building products, automating workflows and sharpening my technical fluency through practice.

whyAi.label: Why AI
whyAi.title: Learning through building, not just reading
paragraphs: My interest in AI began as a customer-facing seller trying to understand a rapidly changing technology. It became more serious when I recognised the difference between being familiar with AI and being genuinely fluent in it.
Since then, I have focused on learning through building, creating applications, automations and structured practice systems rather than relying only on courses or passive study.

My goal is not to present myself as a software engineer. It is to become the kind of AI GTM professional who can understand the product, ask better questions and connect technical possibilities to real customer outcomes.

projects.title: OpenAI BDR Interviewer Buddy
projects.summary: A record-and-review practice app that helps Max prepare AI concepts, OpenAI products, and real life business value.
projects.galleryDescription: Voice practice and structured feedback for OpenAI interview fluency.
description: This app is not a generic quiz tool. It is an interview-performance training system built around daily five-question voice sessions, topic mastery, retry logic, and commercially grounded feedback.

The browser captures a single answer, sends temporary audio to the backend, transcribes it with OpenAI speech-to-text, then discards the raw audio. The transcript is evaluated with structured AI scoring across technical accuracy, simple explanation, business relevance, OpenAI positioning, interview structure, and concision.

The app also includes production plumbing for Supabase persistence, private login placeholders, daily practice, manual practice modes, topic mastery, and a future freshness review queue for approved OpenAI and competitor source updates.
highlights: Backend-only OpenAI API calls so keys never touch the browser.
Daily adaptive flow from foundation to business translation, scenario, objection handling, and BDR close.
Transcript-first feedback with stronger answer, factual corrections, retry prompts, and mastery updates.
Designed for Singapore and APAC commercial fluency, not generic AI trivia.

caseStudySections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Interviewer Buddy is a private voice-practice app built to prepare for AI GTM interviews.

It generates daily interview questions covering AI fundamentals, products, commercial use cases, prospect scenarios and objection handling. Users answer aloud, then receive AI-powered transcription, scoring, critique, and practical guidance for improving the next attempt.

The app tracks progress across practice sessions, identifies weaker topics, preserves past question sets for later completion, and incorporates official OpenAI sources to keep selected topics current.

caseStudySections.title: Why I Built It
paragraphs: I was inspired to build Interviewer Buddy after reaching the final round for an OpenAI GTM role and identifying AI and technical fluency as an area I needed to strengthen.
Reflecting back on how I prepared, I realised that I was focused on cramming AI concepts and rehearsing questions, rather than improving the way I think, communicate and respond under pressure.

Instead of relying on passive study, I built a daily voice-practice system that makes me explain AI concepts, work through realistic customer scenarios, connect technical capabilities to commercial value, and handle objections aloud.
This project reflects how I approach a steep learning curve: turn feedback into a structured practice loop, make improvement measurable, and keep iterating until the gap closes.

caseStudySections.title: Outcomes and Learnings
paragraphs: Interviewer Buddy became both a practical preparation tool and a hands-on way for me to learn how AI products are built with Codex.
This project taught me that:
items: The best AI products begin with a real user problem, not simply an excuse to use AI.
Explaining a concept aloud reveals gaps that passive reading can easily hide.
Adaptive questioning creates a more realistic learning experience than static question banks.
Feedback is most useful when it explains the evidence behind an assessment and gives the user a clear next step.
AI-generated coaching should support human judgement rather than present itself as an objective hiring verdict.
Codex became far more useful once I stopped treating it like an autocomplete tool and started treating it as a collaborative engineering partner.
The user must still remain responsible for product scope, decisions, testing, and quality.

caseStudySections.title: How This Project Changed Me
paragraphs: When I started building Interviewer Buddy, I saw myself primarily as an enterprise seller trying to become more technically fluent.
Through the process, I began thinking more naturally in terms of user problems, product decisions, testing, iteration, and responsible AI use.
The project reinforced one lesson more than any other: building is one of the fastest ways to learn.
Interviewer Buddy began as a tool to prepare for another interview. It became a practical example of how I now respond when I encounter a gap in my skills: I build my way through it.

projects.title: Do Already?
projects.summary: An accountability assistant that turns The Wife's instructions on Telegram into actionable tasks, while keeping it playful with a reward system.
projects.galleryDescription: A playful mobile-first dashboard for keeping promises made at home.
description: Do Already? turns a consented Telegram instruction from a partner into an editable household promise.
GPT-5.6 Luna extracts structured task details, routes clear tasks automatically, and asks for approval on medium-confidence messages. Low-confidence chat is ignored.
A mobile-first dashboard tracks tasks, completion or misses, and a partner-chosen reward without retaining original messages.
highlights: Clear requests can be added to the active task list automatically, while medium-confidence requests stay private until approved.
Each missed promise adds $100 toward a partner-chosen, editable reward without automating a payment or consequence.
Only structured task data is stored; original Telegram message text is not retained.
The optional Telegram flow is limited to a consented private group and allowlisted people.
projects.role: Product owner, designer, and builder for a focused Build Week experiment.

caseStudySections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Do Already? is a playful, accountability assistant for everyday household commitments.

When a Telegram message is received, the server calls the OpenAI Responses API with GPT-5.6 Luna to determine if it is an instruction, which will then be converted into a task. The dashboard then makes it easy to record whether it was done or missed, keeps the agreed reward visible so the experience remains light-hearted, clear, and motivating.

caseStudySections.title: Why I Built It
paragraphs: For OpenAI Build Week, I chose the "Apps for your life" category.
Looking at how much I use AI at work and personal projects, I thought it would be fun to build something that involves my wife. As the saying goes, "Happy Wife, Happy Life".
As an aspiring AI GTM seller, I reflected deeply and identified a small, well-contained problem with a huge negative impact: I always forget to do the tasks my wife asks me to.
Till now, we had to rely on my empty promises to remember my tasks better. I wanted to test whether AI could turn our daily conversations into tasks.
The result is deliberately narrow: it helps me keep promises made at home, while keeping the process and outcome in my hands.

caseStudySections.title: Outcomes and Learnings
paragraphs: The project became a working mobile-first loop: a Telegram message can become a structured promise, clear requests are saved automatically, uncertain ones receive private approval, and ordinary chat is ignored.

I learned that reliable AI automation depends as much on boundaries as on extraction quality. Confidence routing, explicit consent, compact context for task updates, and a clear fallback path made the flow more trustworthy.

Privacy shaped the product too. Only structured task data is stored; original Telegram message text is not retained, and the optional integration is limited to a consented private group and allowlisted people.

caseStudySections.title: How This Project Changed Me
paragraphs: Do Already? pushed me to think beyond a model call and toward the experience around it: user consent, edge cases, recovery paths, and the tone a product creates.
Codex helped turn the idea into a focused Build Week project, from narrowing the MVP to implementing confidence routing, D1 persistence, and a mobile-first dashboard.
It reinforced that a good AI product does not have to start as a large platform. A small, recurring frustration can be enough when the workflow is clear and the human stays in control.

projects.title: Bus 15 Telegram Alert
projects.summary: A weekday automation that checks real-time Bus 15 arrivals and sends Max a Telegram alert with the next catchable bus and when to leave home.
projects.galleryDescription: Real-time Bus 15 alerts with practical leave-time guidance.
description: This automation was built around a practical morning decision: which Bus 15 can Max actually catch after a 10-minute walk and a two-minute buffer?

A Supabase Edge Function checks the official LTA DataMall Bus Arrival endpoint on weekday mornings, then sends the next and subsequent arrival times through Telegram with a clear leave-time recommendation.

Supabase Cron is the live scheduler because GitHub Actions scheduled jobs were too unreliable for a time-sensitive alert. Telegram reply commands can pause, stop, or resume alerts for the current day.
highlights: Uses live LTA arrival data rather than scraping a transit webpage.
Recommends the best catchable bus instead of merely forwarding arrival times.
Supports Telegram pause, stop, and resume commands for the current day.
Uses Supabase Cron for dependable weekday-morning execution.
projects.role: Product owner and builder for a personal commuting workflow.

caseStudySections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Bus 15 Telegram Alert is a personal automation that turns real-time public-transport information into a practical morning decision.

It calls Singapore's Land Transport Authority API, checks Bus 15 arrivals at my usual stop, and sends a concise Telegram message showing the next two buses, along with a recommendation on when I should leave home.
The project also supports one-off lookups in Telegram using a simple command such as "Bus 20 76953".

caseStudySections.title: Why I Built It
paragraphs: Checking bus timings while carrying a toddler and three bags is an unnecessary morning headache. A missed bus can mean my son arriving 20 minutes late for school and me starting work 20 minutes behind schedule. The real question was never simply "When is the next bus?", but "Which bus can I realistically catch, and when should I leave?".
I wanted that decision delivered automatically in an app I already use, rather than repeatedly opening a transport app and calculating the timing in my head.

caseStudySections.title: Outcomes and Learnings
paragraphs: The project evolved from a basic GitHub Actions script into a more reliable Vercel, QStash, Upstash Redis, and Telegram workflow.

Along the way, I learned that automation is not just about getting code to run. It is also about making schedules dependable, preventing duplicate alerts, protecting secrets, handling failures, and giving the user control when plans change.
The result is a small system that now fits naturally into my morning.

caseStudySections.title: How This Project Changed Me
paragraphs: This project changed how I think about AI-assisted development.
I used to assume that automation had to begin with a large idea or elaborate product. Instead, I learned that a narrow, recurring frustration can be an excellent starting point.
It also taught me to think more like a product owner: identify the real decision the user needs to make, simplify the experience around that decision, and improve reliability through iteration.
Most importantly, it gave me confidence that I can take a personal workflow from an idea, through several imperfect versions, into a working tool that I genuinely rely on.

projects.title: Daily AI Newsletter
projects.summary: A scheduled ChatGPT task that researches key AI developments and emails Max a concise daily briefing.
projects.galleryDescription: A daily, source-linked AI briefing delivered by email.
description: This personal automation reviews important AI developments from roughly the last 24 hours, prioritising OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and DeepMind, and material policy, market, safety, infrastructure, and talent moves.
Each email starts with a short executive summary, then covers the major labs, other important AI moves, and why the developments matter for OpenAI.
The scheduled task sends the newsletter directly to Max's Gmail account, includes source links, and closes with a watchlist for the next 24 to 72 hours.
highlights: Researches and links to reliable primary or high-quality sources.
Turns a broad news cycle into a brief designed for fast personal reading.
Separates what happened from why it matters for OpenAI.
Maintains a short watchlist rather than filling space with low-signal news.
projects.role: Workflow designer for a personal learning habit.

caseStudySections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Daily AI Newsletter is a scheduled briefing that delivers a concise summary of the AI developments most relevant to me.

Each edition scans recent updates across foundation models, AI products, enterprise adoption, go-to-market developments, and the companies I am actively following. It then filters and summarises the most important stories into a structured email that I can review before starting the day.

Rather than presenting a generic list of headlines, the newsletter focuses on why each development matters, how it may affect enterprise customers, and what it could mean for someone building a career in AI go-to-market.

caseStudySections.title: Why I Built It
paragraphs: There was no shortage of news, product announcements, research updates, and opinions. The real challenge was deciding what deserved my attention and how each development connected to the commercial conversations I wanted to become better at having.
I found myself checking multiple sources throughout the day, saving articles I rarely returned to, and consuming information without consistently turning it into useful understanding.

I built the newsletter to create a more deliberate learning habit. Instead of repeatedly searching for updates, I receive one focused briefing that helps me understand what changed, why it matters, and which topics are worth exploring further.

caseStudySections.title: Outcomes and Learnings
paragraphs: The most useful outcome has been consistency.

The newsletter gives me a dependable way to stay informed without allowing news consumption to take over my day. It has also helped me build a broader view of the AI market by connecting technical developments with product strategy, enterprise adoption, competitive positioning, and go-to-market implications.
Through the project, I learned that a useful briefing is not defined by the number of articles it includes. Its value comes from prioritisation, context, and relevance.

I also learned that automated research still requires clear editorial judgement. Sources must be assessed carefully, repeated stories need to be removed, and important announcements should be distinguished from speculation or noise.

caseStudySections.title: How This Project Changed Me
paragraphs: This project changed the way I approach learning.
I previously treated staying informed as a reactive activity: read whatever appeared in my feed, save interesting links, and hope the important ideas stayed with me.
Building the newsletter pushed me to define the subjects I genuinely care about, create a repeatable system around them, and connect daily developments to longer-term career goals.
It also reinforced that AI is most useful when it helps create better habits rather than simply producing more information.

The newsletter began as a way to keep up with a fast-moving industry. It has since become part of how I steadily build the market awareness, technical fluency, and commercial perspective required for a career in AI.
